Q. A nurse is caring for a client who is 2 days postoperative following a total hip arthroplasty. The client suddenly becomes anxious and reports shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. Assessment reveals: HR 124/min, RR 30/min, BP 98/62 mmHg, SpO₂ 88% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
A · Incorrect
Administer the prescribed PRN anxiolytic.
Treats the symptom of anxiety, not the cause. Sedating the client can mask worsening hypoxia and delay recognition of a life-threatening event — never treat anxiety first when vitals suggest a physiologic emergency.
B · Correct
Apply supplemental oxygen and notify the provider immediately.
Sudden dyspnea + pleuritic pain + tachycardia + hypoxia after immobility is the classic pulmonary embolism triad. Airway/breathing come first (ABCs): stabilize oxygenation, then escalate for imaging (CT-PA) and anticoagulation.
C · Incorrect
Reposition the client to the left lateral Sims’ position.
This is the correct positioning for a suspected venous air embolism, not a PE — a different diagnosis with a different mechanism. Applying it here delays oxygen and provider notification without addressing the actual clot.
D · Incorrect
Encourage the client to use the incentive spirometer.
Useful for preventing atelectasis and pneumonia postoperatively, but far too passive for an acute hypoxic emergency — it does nothing to correct the SpO₂ of 88% right now.
